h1. Section 9: Understanding Hermes Engine Benefits

The JavaScript engine is a fundamental part of any React Native application, responsible for executing your application's logic. Hermes is an open-source JavaScript engine specifically optimized for running React Native apps. This section explores what Hermes is, its key benefits, and how it contributes to better performance for applications like SpeedyMeds.

bq. 🛣️ *(All Learners):* Understanding the role of the JavaScript engine, and Hermes in particular, helps in making informed decisions about your app's architecture and appreciating the underlying technology that boosts its performance.

h2. Conceptual Content: What is Hermes?

Hermes is a JavaScript engine developed by Meta (formerly Facebook) with a focus on improving the performance of React Native applications, especially on Android, though its availability and usage on iOS have also become standard.

Unlike general-purpose JavaScript engines like V8 (used in Chrome and Node.js) or JavaScriptCore (JSC, used by default in older React Native versions or on iOS if Hermes isn't enabled), Hermes is specifically tailored for the React Native environment. Its design priorities include:

h2. Fast Startup

Minimizing the time it takes for the app to become interactive.
h2. Reduced Memory Usage

Optimizing for memory efficiency on mobile devices.
h2. Smaller Application Size

Contributing to a smaller overall app footprint.

h3. Key Benefits of Using Hermes
# *Improved Start-up Time (Time To Interactive - TTI):*
*** Hermes achieves this primarily through *Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation*. During your app's build process, Hermes compiles JavaScript source code into optimized bytecode. This pre-compiled bytecode can be loaded and executed much faster by the Hermes engine at runtime compared to parsing and compiling raw JavaScript on the fly.
*** For SpeedyMeds, this means users can access their medication lists or emergency contact information more quickly after launching the app.
# *Reduced Memory Usage:*
*** Hermes is designed with memory efficiency in mind. It employs strategies like an optimized garbage collector tailored for React Native's object lifecycle and patterns, and by avoiding JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation which can consume more memory.
*** This is particularly beneficial on resource-constrained Android devices.
# *Smaller App Size (for the JavaScript part):*
*** The bytecode generated by Hermes can be more compact than the equivalent JavaScript source code, contributing to a smaller download size for your app's JavaScript assets.

h3. How Hermes Achieves These Benefits

h2. Bytecode Pre-compilation

As mentioned, JavaScript is compiled to bytecode during the app build, not when the user launches the app. This shifts the compilation overhead from runtime to build time.
h2. No JIT Compiler

Traditional JS engines often use Just-In-Time (JIT) compilers to optimize hot code paths at runtime. While JIT can lead to peak performance for long-running tasks, it adds to startup overhead and memory usage. Hermes forgoes a JIT compiler, focusing instead on efficient bytecode execution.
h2. Optimized Garbage Collector (GC)

Hermes features a GC designed to work well with typical React Native memory allocation patterns, aiming for lower pause times and better memory management.
h2. Focus on ES6 Standards

Hermes implements modern JavaScript (ES6+) standards but may not prioritize experimental or less common language features if they compromise its core goals of startup performance and efficiency.

h3. Hermes Availability

h2. Android

Hermes is the default JavaScript engine for new React Native projects (0.64+) on Android.
h2. iOS

Hermes can be enabled for iOS and is the default for newer React Native versions (0.70+). Expo projects generally default to using Hermes on both platforms when available and supported by the SDK version.
h2. Expo

Expo SDK versions generally manage Hermes integration. For newer SDKs (e.g., 46+), Hermes is often enabled by default where supported.

h3. Debugging with Hermes

As covered in Section 7, Hermes has specific debugging support:

h2. Flipper

Provides the "Hermes Debugger" plugin for direct JavaScript debugging on the device/emulator, including breakpoints, stepping, and variable inspection.
h2. Chrome DevTools (with a proxy)

It's possible to debug Hermes using Chrome DevTools by connecting to the Hermes debugger through a special inspector protocol. Flipper often facilitates this connection.

bq. 📲 *(Native Developers):*
*Comparison:* Think of Hermes as a specialized virtual machine (VM) and runtime for React Native\'s JavaScript, much like the Android Runtime (ART) is for Kotlin/Java bytecode on Android, or the Swift/Objective-C runtime and LLVM compilation stack on iOS. Its Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation of JavaScript to bytecode is conceptually similar to how native code is compiled to machine-readable formats before an app is deployed.
*Key Takeaway:* Hermes aims to bring some of the performance characteristics typically associated with compiled native languages (like faster startup due to pre-compilation and optimized bytecode) to the JavaScript layer within the React Native framework.
*Source:* {{[https://source.android.com/docs/core/dalvik|Android Developer Docs: Android Runtime (ART) and Dalvik]}}, {{[https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/about-the-swift-compilation-process|Apple Developer Docs: About the Swift  Compilation Process]}}

bq. 🌐 *(Web Developers):*
*Comparison:* Unlike general-purpose browser JavaScript engines (like V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore) which often employ sophisticated Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation to achieve peak performance for dynamic web page content and long-running scripts, Hermes prioritizes mobile app startup time (TTI) and resource constraints (memory, app size). It does this by focusing on Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation to optimized bytecode and forgoing a JIT compiler.
*Key Takeaway:* Hermes makes different architectural trade-offs compared to browser engines. It\'s less about achieving the absolute maximum JavaScript execution speed for complex, long-running computations and more about ensuring the React Native app launches quickly and runs smoothly within the typical mobile usage patterns.
*Source:* {{[https://v8.dev/|V8 JavaScript Engine Documentation]}}, {{[https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/JavaScript_technologies_overview|MDN Web Docs: JavaScript technologies overview]}}

h2. Procedural Content: Managing Hermes

h3. Checking if Hermes is Enabled
# *React Native Projects (Non-Expo CLI / Bare Workflow):*

h3. Android

Look in your {{android/app/build.gradle}} file. You should see a line like {{enableHermes: true}} or a property {{hermesEnabled = true}}.
h3. iOS

In your {{ios/Podfile}}, you might see {{:hermes_enabled => true}} as part of the React Native pod configuration. Also, the build logs in Xcode might indicate if Hermes is being used.
# *Expo Projects (Managed Workflow or {{expo-dev-client}}):*
*** Hermes is generally enabled by default in recent Expo SDK versions for both Android and iOS builds. You can specify the {{jsEngine}} in your {{app.json}} or {{app.config.js}} file:

{code:language=js}
    // app.json
    {
      "expo": {
        "name": "SpeedyMeds",
        // ... other configurations
        "android": {
          // ...
          "jsEngine": "hermes"
        },
        "ios": {
          // ...
          "jsEngine": "hermes"
        }
      }
    }
{code}
*** If `jsEngine` is not specified, Expo usually defaults to Hermes for builds. For development with Expo Go, it traditionally used JavaScriptCore, but this is evolving. For the most accurate on-device performance matching production, use a development build (`expo-dev-client`).

h3. Enabling Hermes (If Not Default)

For older React Native projects or if you've explicitly disabled it:

h2. Android

In `android/app/build.gradle`, find the `project.ext.react` block and set `enableHermes: true`.

{code:language=gradle}
project.ext.react = [
    enableHermes: true,  // clean and rebuild if changing
    // ... other settings
]
{code}

Or, within the `defaultConfig` or a specific build type:

{code:language=gradle}
android {
  // ...
  defaultConfig {
    // ...
    ndk {
      // ...
    }
    project.ext.set("react", [
        hermesEnabled: true
    ])
  }
}
{code}

The exact syntax can vary slightly between React Native versions. Always refer to official React Native documentation.

h2. iOS

In your `ios/Podfile`, ensure the `:hermes_enabled` flag is set to `true` for the React Native pod configuration. Example:

{code:language=ruby}
target 'YourAppName' do
  # ... other pods
  use_react_native!(
    :path => config[:reactNativePath],
    # to enable hermes on iOS, change `false` to `true` and then install pods
    :hermes_enabled => true
  )
  # ...
end
{code}

After changing, run `pod install` in the `ios` directory and rebuild your project.

h2. Expo

As shown above, use the `jsEngine: "hermes"` setting in `app.json` or `app.config.js` for Android and iOS specific sections.

{note}
After enabling or disabling Hermes, you usually need to clean your build artifacts and rebuild the native application entirely (e.g., `cd android && ./gradlew clean && cd .. && npx react-native run-android`, or similar for iOS in Xcode).
{note}
